exercises.prompt: A script starts with `use strict;` and later, by mistake, assigns to `$cuont` instead of the declared `$count`. What happens when you run it?

options.label: Perl refuses to compile the program and names the undeclared variable
options.feedback: Yes. Under `use strict`, every variable must be declared, so the misspelling is a compile-time error and no line of the program runs.

options.label: It runs, and `$cuont` is quietly created as a new global variable
options.feedback: Not yet. That is what happens *without* `use strict`, which is exactly the bug strict exists to catch.

options.label: It runs, but prints a warning when `$cuont` is used
options.feedback: Not yet. Warnings are for legal-but-suspicious code. An undeclared variable under strict is not legal at all, so it is an error, not a warning.

options.label: Perl corrects the spelling to `$count` automatically
options.feedback: Not yet. Perl never guesses which variable you meant; it suggests that you may have forgotten a `my` declaration.

hints: Is an undeclared variable illegal or merely suspicious under strict?
When does Perl check a whole file for problems like this: before running, or while running?
exercises.solution: `use strict` requires every variable to be declared, usually with `my`. Perl compiles the whole file before running any of it, so it reports `Global symbol "$cuont" requires explicit package name` and aborts. Nothing runs, which is the point: the typo is found immediately instead of producing a silently wrong answer.

feedback.message: Not yet. Look at the quotes around the second string: single quotes do not interpolate.

hints: The dot joins two strings. Which of them is in double quotes?
exercises.solution: The first string is double-quoted, so `$lang` becomes `Perl`, giving `I know Perl ` (with a trailing space). The second is single-quoted, so `$n` stays as the two characters `$n`. Joined, and with `say` adding a newline: `I know Perl and $n more`.

feedback.message: Close. The minus sign in `%-6s` means left-aligned: the padding goes after the text.
Close. `%4d` without a minus sign right-aligns the number.
Not yet. In Perl, `2 / 3` is ordinary division, not integer division.

hints: `%-6s` pads the string to 6 characters, on the right.
`%4d` pads the integer to 4 characters, on the left. `%.2f` rounds to two decimals.
exercises.solution: `%-6s` prints `ab` left-aligned in 6 columns: `ab` followed by four spaces. `%4d` prints `42` right-aligned in 4 columns: two spaces then `42`. `2 / 3` is 0.666…, and `%.2f` rounds it to `0.67`. So the line is `ab    |  42|0.67`.

feedback.message: Not yet. Perl does not treat the whole string as zero: it uses the number at its start.

hints: `+` needs numbers, so Perl converts the string.
Perl reads as much of a number as it can from the start of the string.
exercises.solution: `+` is numeric, so Perl converts `"7 days"` to a number by reading the leading digits: 7. The sum is 10. Because `use warnings` is on, Perl also prints `Argument "7 days" isn't numeric in addition (+)` to standard error, telling you the conversion was lossy.

answers: The CAMEL has 5 letters no newline here
hints: `say` and `print` both print all their arguments one after another, but only `say` adds a newline.
exercises.solution: The first `say` prints its five arguments with nothing between them: `The CAMEL has 5 letters`, then a newline. `print "no newline"` prints without a newline, so the final `say " here"` continues the same line: `no newline here`. The two lines are `The CAMEL has 5 letters` and `no newline here`.

exercises.prompt: Which command shows, in your terminal, the documentation for Perl's built-in function `split`?
hints: It has a switch for built-in **f**unctions.
exercises.solution: `perldoc -f split` shows the entry for `split` from perlfunc. Similarly `perldoc -v` looks up a special variable, `perldoc -q` searches the FAQ, and `perldoc Some::Module` shows a module's documentation.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about Perl and Raku is accurate?

options.label: Raku began as Perl 6 but is a separate language; Perl 5 code does not run on it
options.feedback: Yes. The project started in 2000 as Perl 6 and was renamed Raku in 2019 to make clear it is a different language.

options.label: Raku is the current version of Perl and replaced Perl 5 in 2019
options.feedback: Not yet. Perl 5 is actively developed, with a new stable release about once a year. Raku is a sibling, not a successor.

options.label: Raku is a CPAN module that adds new syntax to Perl 5
options.feedback: Not yet. Raku has its own compiler (Rakudo), its own module ecosystem and its own syntax.

options.label: Raku is the name of Perl's regular expression engine
options.feedback: Not yet. Raku does have its own powerful pattern language, but Raku is the name of the whole language.

hints: Ask whether a Perl 5 script runs unchanged under the other language.
exercises.solution: Raku is the language that was designed as Perl 6. It turned out so different that it was renamed in 2019. Perl 5, the language this course teaches, continues independently; when people say "Perl" they mean Perl 5.

exercises.prompt: Which of these statements about perl's command-line switches are true? Choose all that apply.

options.label: `-e` runs the code given as the next argument
`-n` loops over input lines without printing them; `-p` loops and prints each line
options.feedback: Yes. `-p` is `-n` plus an automatic print at the end of each pass.

options.label: `-i` edits files in place, and `-i.bak` keeps a backup
options.feedback: Yes. That is how `perl -pi.bak -e 's/a/b/g' *.txt` edits files safely.

options.label: `-a` turns on `use strict` automatically
options.feedback: Not yet. `-a` is autosplit: it splits each input line into the array `@F`.

hints: One of the switches splits lines into fields.
Look again at what -n, -p and -i do with each line.
exercises.solution: `-e` gives the program on the command line, `-n` and `-p` wrap it in a loop over input lines (`-p` also prints), `-i` edits in place with an optional backup suffix, and `-a` splits each line into `@F`. None of them enables strict.
